front: Name the three structures a plant cell has that an animal cell does not.
answer: Cell wall / Chloroplasts / Permanent vacuole
title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

front: Name the five sub-cellular structures found in a typical animal cell.
answer: Nucleus / Cytoplasm / Cell membrane / Mitochondria / Ribosomes
title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

front: How does the long, thin extension of a root hair cell help the plant?
answer: It increases the surface area of the cell, so more water and mineral ions can be absorbed from the soil.
title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

front: Why is a coverslip lowered onto a slide at an angle?
answer: Lowering it at an angle stops air bubbles being trapped underneath, and trapped bubbles would distort the image seen down the microscope.
title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

front: Name the four factors that affect the rate of diffusion.
answer: Concentration gradient / Temperature / Surface area of the membrane / Distance the particles travel
title: Cell Division and Transport

front: Name the three ways substances move across a cell membrane.
answer: Diffusion / Osmosis / Active transport
title: Cell Division and Transport

front: How does mitosis produce two daughter cells that are genetically identical?
answer: The DNA is copied first, then one full set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell before it divides in two.
title: Cell Division and Transport

front: Why can a root hair cell take in mineral ions when the soil around it is more dilute?
answer: Active transport uses energy from respiration to move the ions against the concentration gradient, from the lower concentration outside to the higher concentration inside.
title: Cell Division and Transport

front: List, from smallest to largest, the five levels of organisation in the human body.
answer: Cells / Tissues / Organs / Organ systems / Organism
title: Organisation and the Digestive System

front: Name the three main types of digestive enzyme.
answer: Amylase / Proteases / Lipases
title: Organisation and the Digestive System

front: Why can only one type of substrate fit into a particular enzyme?
answer: Each enzyme has an active site with a unique shape, so only a substrate with a matching shape can fit into it.
title: Organisation and the Digestive System

front: Why must large food molecules be broken down before the body can use them?
answer: Large food molecules are insoluble, so they must be broken into smaller soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood.
title: Organisation and the Digestive System

front: Name the four components of blood.
answer: Red blood cells / White blood cells / Platelets / Plasma
title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

front: Name the three types of blood vessel.
answer: Arteries / Veins / Capillaries
title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

front: How does a build-up of fatty material in the coronary arteries lead to a heart attack?
answer: The fatty layers narrow the arteries and reduce blood flow, so the heart muscle may not receive enough oxygen.
title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

front: Why does blood pass through the heart twice on each circuit of the body?
answer: The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the left side then pumps the oxygenated blood on to the rest of the body.
title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

front: Name the four factors that affect the rate of transpiration.
answer: Temperature / Humidity / Air movement / Light intensity
title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

front: Name the five main plant tissues.
answer: Epidermal tissue / Palisade mesophyll / Spongy mesophyll / Xylem / Phloem
title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

front: How does transpiration move water from the roots to the leaves?
answer: Water evaporates and diffuses out of the leaves through the stomata, creating a transpiration stream that pulls water up the xylem from the roots.
title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

front: Why does a risk factor not always prove that something causes a disease?
answer: A risk factor is only correlated with the disease: it makes the disease more likely, but correlation does not always prove causation.
title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

front: Name the four main types of pathogen.
answer: Bacteria / Viruses / Fungi / Protists
title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences

front: Name the three ways white blood cells attack pathogens.
answer: Engulfing and digesting pathogens / Producing antibodies / Producing antitoxins
title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences

front: Why does someone often fall ill the first time a pathogen enters, but not the second time?
answer: The first time, white blood cells need several days to make the right antibodies; memory cells make that response far faster the second time.
title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences

front: How does a virus destroy the cell it infects?
answer: It takes over the cell's machinery to make copies of itself, and this often destroys the cell in the process.
title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences

front: Name, in order, the three stages a new drug must pass through before it can be used.
answer: Preclinical testing on cells and animals / Clinical trials on volunteers then patients / Peer review and approval
items: Preclinical testing on cells and animals
Clinical trials on volunteers then patients
title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

front: Name the three actions that slow the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
answer: Only prescribe antibiotics when necessary / Always complete the full course / Restrict agricultural use of antibiotics
title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

front: Why do painkillers not cure an infection?
answer: Painkillers only treat the symptoms, such as pain and inflammation; they do not kill the pathogen causing the infection.
title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

front: Why is neither the patient nor the doctor told who is receiving the real drug?
answer: Keeping both of them unaware of who receives the drug and who receives the placebo removes bias from the results.
title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

front: Name the three limiting factors for the rate of photosynthesis.
answer: Light intensity / Carbon dioxide concentration / Temperature
title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

front: Name the five ways a plant uses the glucose it makes in photosynthesis.
answer: Respiration to release energy / Stored as starch / Making cellulose for cell walls / Making amino acids for proteins / Making lipids stored in seeds
title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

front: Why does adding more light eventually stop increasing the rate of photosynthesis?
answer: Another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, becomes the limiting factor, so extra light can no longer raise the rate.
title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

front: Why does lactic acid build up in the muscles during intense exercise?
answer: The muscles cannot get enough oxygen for aerobic respiration alone, so anaerobic respiration also takes place and produces lactic acid.
title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

front: Name the four precautions taken when growing bacteria to keep unwanted microorganisms out.
answer: Sterilise all equipment before use / Tape the lid without sealing it / Work near a Bunsen flame / Incubate at no more than 25 °C
items: Tape the lid without sealing it
title: Culturing Microorganisms and Plant Disease

front: Name the five signs that a plant may be diseased.
answer: Stunted growth / Spots on leaves / Areas of decay or rot / Discolouration / Malformed stems or leaves
title: Culturing Microorganisms and Plant Disease

front: Why is an agar plate opened next to a lit Bunsen burner?
answer: The flame creates an updraught that carries airborne microorganisms away from the open plate, so they do not contaminate the culture.
title: Culturing Microorganisms and Plant Disease

front: How does rose black spot reduce a plant's ability to photosynthesise?
answer: The black spots make affected leaves turn yellow and drop early, so the plant has less leaf area left for photosynthesis.
title: Culturing Microorganisms and Plant Disease

front: List, in order, the five steps used to make monoclonal antibodies.
answer: Inject a mouse with the antigen / Collect lymphocytes from the spleen / Fuse them with tumour cells / Screen the hybridomas for the antibody / Clone and grow the chosen cells
items: Inject a mouse with the antigen
Screen the hybridomas for the antibody
Clone and grow the chosen cells
title: Monoclonal Antibodies

front: Name the three limitations of monoclonal antibody treatments.
answer: Unexpected side effects / Expensive to develop and produce / No miracle cures yet
title: Monoclonal Antibodies

front: Why is a mouse injected with the target antigen at the start of the process?
answer: Its immune system responds by making lymphocytes that produce antibodies against that antigen, and those lymphocytes are then collected and fused.
title: Monoclonal Antibodies

front: How do scientists use monoclonal antibodies to see where a protein sits inside a cell?
answer: The antibodies are tagged with a fluorescent dye and bind only to that protein, showing exactly where it is in the cell.
title: Monoclonal Antibodies
